cards.title: Voice Memo Test for Topic Selection
cards.summary: Filter content ideas by whether you'd naturally tell a friend about them in a 60-second voice memo.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product stories, email campaign angles or blog topics to publish for your store's audience.
steps: Before writing any piece of content, record a 60-second voice memo as if telling a friend: 'Hey, did you hear what happened — this thing happened and people are freaking out because...'

If the topic doesn't survive that filter — if you'd never bring it up unprompted to a friend — don't write about it. Applied to ecommerce: if a new product drop, ingredient change or brand story wouldn't make you excitedly text a friend, it won't excite a stranger either.
Use the recorded memo as your first draft. The natural spoken version is usually the right structure and tone. Transcribe and lightly edit rather than starting from a blank formal draft.

The source's example: James Clear-style Milk Road newsletter writers were writing boring, fluffy drafts — the fix was having them send voice memos instead of written drafts, which immediately clarified which topics were worth sending.
caveats: The voice memo is a filter and structural guide, not a finished copy block. Transcription still needs editing for clarity, facts and brand fit.
Works for editorial and social content, not for mandatory transactional copy like order confirmations.

cards.title: Write to One Person, Not a Crowd
cards.summary: Direct all content and copy to a single named individual to keep it natural and reduce writer anxiety.
cards.use_when: Drafting store newsletters, product descriptions or landing page copy that is intended for a broad audience but risks sounding corporate.
steps: Pick one specific person — a colleague, a real customer segment you know well, or a fictional composite — and write the piece as if it is only for them.
The source's tip from selling The Hustle (approx. 2M subscribers): new writers got nervous when writing to millions. Instructing them to 'write to Sam' — one person — immediately improved output.
Adjust tone per person type: if you're writing about sustainable skincare to a skeptical customer, phrase it the way you'd explain it to that skeptic in a one-to-one conversation.
Let it be a coincidence that many others read it. The single-recipient framing keeps the language direct and conversational, which the source argues converts better than mass-market register.
caveats: This framing helps voice, not SEO keyword targeting. For product pages where search intent matters, combine conversational copy with required keyword coverage.
Different personas need different 'one persons' — segment communications rather than picking one person for all audiences.

cards.title: Aim for a 6th–8th Grade Reading Level
cards.summary: Write store content at a 6th–8th grade reading level; simpler copy is more effective even on complex topics.
cards.use_when: Editing email campaigns, product descriptions or landing pages intended for broad consumer audiences including busy readers.
steps: Set a target reading level: source says you can go as low as 4th grade but 6th–8th grade is the sweet spot for most consumer writing.
Use an automated readability checker (source references the Hemingway app — verify current interface and availability) to score drafts before publishing.
Apply tactics the tool flags: cut adverbs, keep sentences short, replace jargon and internal terminology with plain words customers already use.

Use reference points: the source cites USA Today at roughly a 4th grade level and the New York Times at roughly a 7th grade level. Even Warren Buffett's writing on complex insurance topics scored around 6th–8th grade.

The source's analysis of Buffett's shareholder letters from 1974 to 2013 shows words per sentence dropping from 17 to 13 and reading level dropping from 10th grade to 4th grade — the more complex his business became, the simpler his writing got.
caveats: Low reading level is a heuristic for broad consumer content, not a law. Technical or professional B2B buyers may expect and tolerate domain-specific language.
Sentence-level simplicity must not remove critical product details, ingredients, sizing or compliance information.

cards.title: Intention and Obstacle: The Core of Any Story
cards.summary: Every effective brand story needs a clear character who wants something and a concrete obstacle in the way.
cards.use_when: Writing founder stories, brand origin pages or ad creative where you need the reader to keep reading past the first line.
steps: Identify the character (founder, customer, product) and name exactly what they want — the intention — on the page.
Name the specific obstacle blocking them — a rejection, a competitor, a supply constraint, skepticism.
Source principle (attributed to Aaron Sorkin): 'I worship at the altar of intention and obstacle' — a story is someone wanting something with something in their way.
Test the draft: pause at any point in the copy and ask 'what does this character want and what's in their way?' If you can't answer immediately, the reader has already lost the thread.

Use a low-stakes version — the source cites Larry David's ability to build story tension from small relatable moments like a dispute in a grocery line — for lifestyle and personality brand content. The emotional stakes just need to feel real to the character.

The source's example: the Hint Water founder story worked because she wanted to build a fruit-flavored water business and be taken seriously, while a Coca-Cola executive dismissed her as 'sweetie.' The intention and obstacle were both explicit in the headline.
caveats: The Hint Water article's commercial success (source says the company spent millions promoting it and it drove tens of millions in sales) is a case study, not a benchmark. It was partly driven by Hint's paid amplification.
Establish intention and obstacle fast — waiting too long to reveal them loses the audience.

cards.title: High Stakes in a Low-Stakes Setting
cards.summary: Make small relatable moments feel emotionally significant to create engaging brand storytelling without needing dramatic events.
cards.use_when: Writing founder content, community posts or ad creative when the product or brand lacks inherent drama.
steps: Identify a genuinely small moment from the brand's history — a shipping mishap, an HOA dispute, a customer complaint, an internal argument over packaging.
Write the narrator's internal emotional stake honestly: what did this feel like, and why did it matter so much at the time?

Get the reader to believe the stakes felt real, not that the stakes objectively were. Source: 'if I can tell you how I was feeling and get you to believe that I thought everything was on the line, I can get you to care about the outcome.'

Referenced examples: a driveway workout dispute with an HOA; a Larry David plot where a character wears a hat specifically to stop strangers talking to him. Both make a tiny thing carry emotional weight.
Apply to ecommerce: a packaging redesign argument, a customer service escalation, first sale disaster stories — all become compelling if the emotional stakes are honestly rendered.
caveats: Used consistently for trivial moments, audiences may find it inauthentic. Reserve for moments where the emotion is genuine.
Source opinion on which examples work best, not an established rule for all audiences.

cards.title: Vary Sentence Length for Rhythm
cards.summary: Alternate short, medium and long sentences to make copy flow and pull readers through.
cards.use_when: Editing store newsletters, landing pages or product descriptions that read flat or monotonous.
steps: Default to short sentences as your baseline. The source's rule: 'anytime you want to use a comma, use a period' — then start the next sentence with 'and' or 'but' if needed for flow.

Introduce variety: after a run of short sentences, insert a medium one, then occasionally a long sentence that 'sings' — the source's phrasing is when the reader is 'rested,' a longer sentence can build energy.

Use the viral example the source cites: 'This sentence has five words. Here are five more. Five-word sentences are fine. But several together become monotonous.' — demonstrating rhythm through text itself.
Use internal dialogue lines as pacing tools: 'you're asking yourself right now,' 'who is this person telling me what to do' — these break up rhythm and re-engage the reader.
Do copywork on writing you find rhythmically strong — physically retype passages to internalize the cadence before writing your own.
caveats: This is a stylist skill. Apply it after the core message is clear — rhythm won't rescue uninteresting content.
Long sentences used poorly read as run-ons just as easily as they read as energy.

cards.title: The 'Letter from the CEO' Sales Page Pattern
cards.summary: A first-person letter from the founder using simple language can serve as an effective sales page format.
cards.use_when: Building or testing the top-of-page copy for a product landing page, especially for a subscription or considered purchase.
steps: Write the page as a direct letter from the founder or CEO in first person, addressed to the reader.
Open with a contrarian or reframing statement about the category, not the product. Source example (Hey.com): 'Email gets a bad rap, but it shouldn't. Email is a treasure.'
Use plain, short sentences to explain why the product exists and what problem it solves in the founder's own voice.

The source's argument for this format: it raises personal stakes (a real human made a claim), which the source argues makes a paid product's value proposition feel more credible than generic marketing copy.
Test this format against your standard benefit-led hero section as a creative variant, particularly for subscription or premium-priced products where the founding rationale is a differentiator.
caveats: Source cites Hey.com's letter as an example of good simple writing, not as a tested conversion benchmark. Treat this as a format hypothesis to test, not a proven lift.
The letter must be genuinely written by or credited to the responsible person — a fabricated founder voice risks trust damage if discovered.

cards.title: The CEO Story That Earns Free Distribution
cards.summary: Stories with an outrage or 'WTF' emotional hook can generate organic pickup and be amplified by the subject.
cards.use_when: Sourcing or writing brand editorial content where you want the subject or third party to share or amplify it.
steps: Identify a moment in the brand or founder story that provokes a distinct emotional reaction — the source's example was a condescending executive calling a female founder 'sweetie' — the headline, from the source's description of the Hint Water post: 'sweetie, help this entrepreneur create a multi-million dollar business.'
Write the story as a genuine editorial piece rather than an advertisement. Source: 'I wrote the blog post not to promote Hint, I wrote it because I thought this was a cool story.'
Structure it so the reason the story matters to you is visible — the source attributes the effectiveness to working backwards from an emotion rather than forward from a product feature.

The commercial mechanism: the subject (Hint) discovered the article and spent millions promoting it, driving tens of millions in sales. This is free distribution earned by writing something the subject wants their audience to read.
Apply to ecommerce: founder origin stories, supply chain battles, category rejection stories. Write them as genuine content and let the subject or the audience amplify.
caveats: The Hint result was an outlier partly driven by paid amplification the author didn't control. Not a dependable outcome.
Stories built on outrage or conflict risk alienating some audience segments and can generate backlash if perceived as manufactured.
The source's claim that 'this article made them tens of millions of dollars in sales' is an unverified case-study claim.

cards.title: Comedy Techniques for Attention and Persuasion
cards.summary: Study comedians' timing, tension and self-deprecation for principles you can apply to brand storytelling and crisis response.
cards.use_when: Writing brand content, apology statements or acquisition creative where you need to hold attention and win the audience's trust.
steps: Study timing: source cites Dave Chappelle and Shane Gillis for pacing — watch specifically for how pauses, setup and callbacks hold attention. Apply the same pacing structure to video ads and story-sequence posts.

Study self-deprecating persuasion (Louis CK post-cancellation): rather than denying, backpedalling or spinning, he acknowledged something awkward using humor ('everybody's got a thing'), which won the audience back on his side. For ecommerce: when a shipping failure or defective batch happens, a self-aware, specific own-the-mistake statement can outperform a corporate mea culpa — the source's framing is that the comedian doesn't deny or spin, he names the thing.

Study story-as-persuasion (Dave Chappelle's 'Unforgiven' segment about his show's royalties): the source describes it as a 'maze that led to one door' — setup so strong the audience arrives at only one conclusion. Apply to acquisition creative where you need viewers to reach a conclusion themselves rather than being told.
caveats: Louis CK and Chappelle examples are the source's analysis of comedy performances, not documented conversion results. Adapt the structural principle, not the specific personal conduct.
Crisis-response humor is high variance — may amplify anger if the initial offense affected customers directly.

cards.title: Find Untapped Content in Engineering/Tech Blog Posts
cards.summary: Detailed, obsessive blog posts from non-marketing authors often contain distinctive content angles.
cards.use_when: Sourcing content ideas or building brand-voice posts when your category's conventional marketing content is saturated.
steps: Monitor aggregator sites like Hacker News for high-ranking posts written by practitioners on topics adjacent to your category, not just your category.

Look for the specific complaint/narrow-obsession angle: the source cites a 10,000-word post about the Kroger grocery app's UX failures ranking on Hacker News — its effectiveness came from deep specific knowledge of one topic, not polished writing.

Use the 'I know nothing about X, but I do know about Y' opening pattern. Source cites this from the Kroger post: 'I know nothing about the grocery industry, but what I do know about is tech and UX.' This frames an outside perspective as an asset and gets readers into the content.
For ecommerce: write a detailed teardown or praise of your own or a competitor's checkout, packaging or customer experience — the specificity is the value, not generalizable assertions.
caveats: This is a sourcing heuristic, not a proven traffic strategy for any specific store.
Niche obsession content reaches a narrower audience — suitable as a distinctive content bet, not a general acquisition channel.

cards.title: 'You Pushed Out': The Personal Monopoly Principle
cards.summary: Content that reflects your genuine interests and opinions attracts a loyal audience no competitor can replicate.
cards.use_when: Defining your store's content voice and deciding which topics the brand should own in its category.
steps: Write about the topics you're genuinely most interested in or nerd out about, even if you suspect few customers care. Source: 'you'll find the people that care about it if you just consistently do that.'

Identify the narrow slice of your category where you have the most passionate, specific knowledge — the source calls this a 'personal monopoly' because nobody else can compete at the thing you care most about.

The source's example: the podcast started by emulating successful formats (Tim Ferriss, How I Built This) and only started working when the host simply spoke about what he genuinely finds interesting — even niche topics like tire rims in North Carolina.

For ecommerce: if you're a skincare brand founded by a formulator who is genuinely obsessed with a specific raw material, that's the content angle — not generic '5 skincare tips' that any competitor can copy.
caveats: Source frames this as a long-term differentiation strategy, not a short-term traffic tactic. It requires consistency and a willingness to accept a narrower initial audience.
Not every founder has a genuine angle that maps to a category — forcing one is worse than a clear, useful generalist content strategy.

cards.title: Copywork as Structured Practice for Better Copy
cards.summary: Retyping well-crafted passages by hand is a repeatable practice method for improving writing style.
cards.use_when: Training yourself or a content team on copy style, especially before producing a batch of store content or ad copy.
steps: Select a passage you find rhythmically strong (the source cites a passage on sentence rhythm and comedy bits like Theo Von's ad copy as examples of distinctive phrasing).
Retype it by hand or type it out word-for-word — not paraphrase. The source says this takes under a minute for a short passage and primes you to write in that style.
Follow up immediately by writing your own copy while the rhythm is fresh, rather than editing or planning first.

Use the source's described structured practice loop: study principle, see the example done well, then try it yourself — repeat with different examples. The source says this repeated practice, not more theory, is what builds improvement.
For ecommerce teams: build a bank of well-written competitor and non-competitor examples and have anyone writing product copy or email campaigns do a short copywork session before drafting.
caveats: This is a skill-building exercise, not a copy-paste production method. Do not reuse copyrighted passages in published content.
The source is a course/podcast host and has commercial interest in popularizing structured writing practice — treat claimed outcomes accordingly.
